AnswerIn.description:
Who answered, and - optionally - which business they are answering for.

**`merchant_id` IS OPTIONAL AND IS CHECKED, WHICH ARE NOT THE SAME THING.**
The contract addresses an action by id alone, so it cannot be required; when
it IS sent it is compared against the row's own owner and a mismatch is
refused before anything is read. Task 16 shipped an audit row that
misdescribed its own mutation because a caller-supplied id was never checked
against the row it named.
AnswerIn.title: AnswerIn

CreateMerchantIn.description:
A business for the demo to be about.

**`category_code` HAS NO DEFAULT, AND THAT IS A SAFETY DECISION RATHER THAN
STRICTNESS.** It used to default to `local_services_plumbing`, and the
argument for that - "a default that is wrong for a real merchant is visible
in `GET /api/merchants/{id}` rather than buried" - was true about *visibility*
and wrong about *consequence*, because this is the one field a SAFETY CHECK
reads.

`workflows.generation.restricted_reason` is `RESTRICTED_VERTICALS.get(
category_code)`, and Blueprint §19 Q4 has it refuse ONBOARDING rather than
fail at launch, so that a trade this platform cannot advertise never has its
website crawled, its account queried or a model asked about it. **The default
was the one value guaranteed to pass that lookup** - plumbing is the demo
vertical, definitionally unrestricted - so a caller who omitted the field
created a merchant that sailed through the gate, and a dental surgery or a
pharmacy onboarded as a plumber gets crawled and written about before anybody
asks what trade it is.

**A silent default answering the question a safety check depends on is not a
default, it is an answer nobody gave.** The console always sends one; a
required field a caller can omit into a false pass is not something a
client-side habit should be standing between.

`autonomy_level` and `monthly_budget_cents` keep their defaults: both are
read by rules that CONSTRAIN what happens, so a wrong one is conservative or
visible rather than permissive.

**AND IT IS NOW CHECKED AGAINST A VOCABULARY, NOT MERELY REQUIRED.** Making
it required closed the half a caller reached by omission; `dental_surgery`
for `healthcare_dental_surgery` still passed, which is the half
`lexicons.py` calls check 11's biggest weakness. `max_length` is the
column's 80 rather than an arbitrary 50, because membership is the check
that matters and a second length limit is a second thing to keep in step.
CreateMerchantIn.title: CreateMerchantIn

SeedIn.description:
Seed a demo account. `reset_platform` is off by default and says why.

A reset empties every PPCWay table and the whole simulated world. That is
what `ppcway demo` does at the start of a run, and it is the right thing
THERE; here it would destroy the other businesses a client had already made
while clicking around. Off unless asked for.
SeedIn.title: SeedIn

SignUpIn.description:
A business registering itself, to connect a Google account it already has.

**THE FIELDS ARE THE ONES NOBODY ELSE CAN ANSWER.** The name is not among
them: it comes from the crawl, because a name read off the merchant's own
website is a fact about the business, whereas a typed one is a claim and a
Google-supplied one would be read back out of a field we populated.

**`currency` IS REQUIRED AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** Every figure on every
screen is formatted in it, so a silent default would misformat all of them
while looking entirely normal - the same defect as `category_code`'s default,
against a field that decides how money is READ rather than whether to
proceed. The Google account carries its own `currency_code`, and the two
disagreeing is a real and currently unchecked state, so guessing this one
would manufacture the mismatch rather than merely fail to detect it.

The guardrail limits are here for the reason `GuardrailConfig`'s own
docstring gives: they are "what this merchant agreed to, not platform
defaults". Writing them on a merchant's behalf would put a version number on
an agreement nobody made, and every audit row records which version
authorised it.
SignUpIn.title: SignUpIn

post.description:
Undo an applied change, through the one door.

`/v1/actions/{id}/revert` and not a local call: the undo is a mutation and
goes through the door like any other, guarded and logged in its own right.

**AN UNDO CAN BE REFUSED AND THAT IS CLAIM 4 HOLDING, NOT FAILING.** Task 32
measured the case: a change made at the per-change cap cannot be reversed,
because undoing a cut of 25% needs a rise of 33% and `delta_limits` will not
allow it. The claim is a disjunction - reversible OR refused loudly with a
reason - so this reports which of the two happened rather than reporting the
second as the first.

get.description:
The trades a business may be created as, with the restricted ones named.

**SERVED SO THAT NOBODY HOLDS A SECOND COPY.** web-ui offered to keep this
list console-side with a checker proving its restriction wording matched
`google.py`-style, character for character. A vocabulary that decides which
trades get refused should not live where nothing upstream validates it, and
`restriction_reason` here is `restricted_reason(code)` verbatim - so the
sentence on the picker and the sentence in a refusal are one string, and
there is nothing for a checker to police.

Restricted trades are INCLUDED. A merchant who cannot find their trade picks
the nearest one that is listed, so hiding a restricted trade does not refuse
it - it launders it into a different category.

What this service can reach, each answered separately.

**THREE FACTS AND NOT ONE BOOLEAN.** "Healthy" would be true of a service
that could reach neither the database nor the gateway and had simply not
tried. Each dependency is asked and each answer stands on its own, so a
client watching this can say which half is down.

post.description:
Create a business with a simulated Google Ads account under the MCC.

**THIS ENDPOINT REQUIRES A SIMULATED DEPLOYMENT AND THAT IS NOT A GAP.** It
creates a merchant AND provisions the Google account it is linked to, which
is only something we can do to a simulator. In a real deployment a merchant
arrives by signing up and connecting their own account through Google's
consent screen, and creating the row without that would leave a business
with a link to an account nobody had authorised.

`ppcway.acceptance.world.seed_merchant` writes the four rows - the merchant,
the link, a first business profile and the guardrail limits - and is used
rather than reproduced. The limits in particular are a judgement about what
a merchant agreed to, and a second copy of them here would be a second set
of numbers to keep in step.

get.description:
The audit log: everything this platform decided about this merchant.

Newest first, every status, each row carrying what changed, the reason it
was proposed, what the guardrails said, and whether an undo may be asked
for. Nothing is filtered out - a rejection is part of the record of what was
done on somebody's behalf, and a log that showed only the successes would be
the wrong shape for the thing it exists to prove.

put.description:
Change how much this platform may do on its own.

**WHAT THIS DOES NOT WRITE, SAID PLAINLY RATHER THAN IMPLIED AWAY.**
Blueprint §8.3 makes autonomy consent a compliance artifact -
`autonomy_consent` records WHO agreed, from which address, against which
guardrail version - and this PoC has no authenticated user to put in it. A
consent row with a made-up user id would be a compliance record that is
worse than none, so none is written, and no response here claims one was.
The level itself is what the guardrails read (`check_autonomy_level` reads
`Merchant.autonomy_level`), so the change is real; what is missing is the
evidence of who asked for it.

The level is validated by `AutonomyIn` against the enum, so an unrecognised
one is a 400 before it reaches a row. That matters more than it looks:
`gateway.actions._autonomy_level` treats a level it does not recognise as
UNEVALUABLE, and every change for that merchant then fails closed forever
with a reason about our own data.

schema.title: Merchant Id
Response Set Autonomy Api Merchants  Merchant Id  Autonomy Put

put.description:
The merchant changes their mind about what to spend in a month.

**A NEW PROFILE VERSION, NOT AN EDIT**, because that is how this platform
records a merchant changing their mind: `load_pacing_state` reads the
highest version, and the earlier one stays as the record of what they had
agreed before. An in-place edit would leave no evidence that the figure the
pacing rule is now correcting towards is not the one the campaign was built
for.

**AND THIS IS WHAT GIVES THE PACING RULE SOMETHING TO SAY.** A campaign
launched by `daily_budget_cents(monthly)` paces almost exactly on target BY
CONSTRUCTION - the daily budget IS the monthly one divided by the month - so
`budget_pacing` correctly proposes nothing about a campaign nobody has
touched, and a demo without this lever shows a merchant an empty approval
queue and no way to fill it. `ppcway.acceptance.story` records the same
measurement and needs the same act.

The campaign's LIVE daily budget is deliberately NOT changed here. That is a
mutation of a merchant's account, it goes through the one door with the
guardrails on it, and the whole point is that the automation proposes it and
the merchant is asked.

get.description:
What Google holds for this business, read through the one door.

The only read this proof of concept makes against a real Google Ads
account. Passed through unshaped, like `/api/quota`: the names, statuses
and figures are Google's, the timestamp is when the door asked, and a
refusal travels inside the answer with Google's reason and one sentence for
the merchant, so the console can say "Google would not answer" rather than
showing a connection error.

post.description:
Log one intent, let the guardrails answer it, then send the four steps.

**THE LAUNCH IS ONE LOGGED DECISION AND FOUR CALLS, AND THE ORDER IS
ENFORCED BY THE DOOR.** A single `CREATE_CAMPAIGN` action whose
`after_values` name the ordered steps authorises the whole sequence;
`/v1/mutate` rebuilds each step from that row and refuses it until its
predecessors have landed with the ids they really created. So this loop
being written correctly is not what makes the order safe.

**PRESSING LAUNCH IS THE APPROVAL.** For an APPROVE_FIRST merchant the
logged intent comes back REQUIRES_APPROVAL, exactly like any other change,
and the approval is applied here - which re-runs every check but autonomy on
a context built now. That is the same shape `ppcway.acceptance.story._launch`
records: demanding PENDING was demanding that the merchant not be asked.

Impressions, clicks, cost and conversions by day.

`days_covered` travels with the rows so a client can say "no figures yet"
rather than drawing an empty chart a merchant reads as zero traffic - the
same distinction `ReconciliationReport.unresolvable` exists for one layer
out: "we looked and there was nothing" is not "we did not look".

Read the website, decide the structure and the bidding, and write a preview.

Nothing is changed on the Google account: the only two calls this makes are
the keyword-ideas read and a pre-flight, and `preflight_campaign_sync` forces
`validate_only` whatever the payload says.

get.description:
Everything waiting for this merchant to answer.

REQUIRES_APPROVAL and nothing else: a queue that also showed rejected or
applied rows would be an audit log with a misleading name, and
`/api/merchants/{id}/actions` is the audit log.

**A LAUNCH IS EXCLUDED, AND THAT IS AN INHERITED GAP RATHER THAN A CHOICE
ABOUT WHAT MERCHANTS SHOULD SEE.** `gateway.actions.submit`'s launch branch
returns without touching the status, so a launch that has been approved AND
CARRIED OUT still reads REQUIRES_APPROVAL for ever - Task 29 disclosed this
in as many words: the audit log cannot tell "waiting for the merchant" from
"the merchant said yes and the launch is under way". Both are unresolved,
which is what the door's gate requires, so the launch proceeds correctly; it
is the READER of the log who is told less than the truth.

Left in, that row sits in the approval queue permanently, asking a merchant
to approve a campaign that is already running - and pressing approve on it
reaches the launch branch again and resolves nothing, so the queue would not
even empty. `is_launch` is the platform's own test for what a launch is
(read from `after_values`, not from the action type, because a
CREATE_CAMPAIGN that is not a sequence is a different thing), so this filter
cannot drift from it. The row is still in `/actions`, with the status the
database actually holds.

post.description:
Apply what the merchant approved. GUARD again, then MUTATE, then RECORD.

LOG is not repeated because the row already exists - that is what an
approval queue is - but every check except autonomy runs again on a context
built NOW, because the account may have moved while the merchant was
thinking. So a 200 here is not necessarily an applied change: read
`applied`, and when it is false read `refusal`.

rejection when somebody asks, months later, why a change did not happen.

post.description:
Register a business that will connect its OWN Google account.

**THIS IS THE REAL-DEPLOYMENT PATH AND IT IS A SECOND ENDPOINT RATHER THAN A
FLAG.** `POST /api/merchants` provisions a Google account and therefore
requires a simulated deployment; conjuring somebody an account they do not
own is a request that should be refused, and that guard stays. The two are
different ACTS, not one act with a branch - and a branch that runs in only
one configuration is how the real-mode path stays untested.

**IT NEVER PROVISIONS, AND THAT IS CHECKED RATHER THAN PROMISED.**
`tests/api/test_signup.py::test_only_the_simulated_endpoint_can_provision_an_account`
walks this module for the functions that reference `provision` and requires
the set to be exactly `{create_merchant}`.

**THE RESTRICTED GATE IS ASKED BEFORE THE CRAWL**, which is §19 Q4's own
ordering and the reason it is written here rather than left to onboarding: a
merchant whose trade this platform cannot advertise should not have their
website read on the way to being told so. Taking a durable Google credential
is strictly more than reading their site, so it must not happen first
either - which is why this endpoint exists at all rather than the console
sending them to Google before we know their trade.

**ONE ROW, NOT `seed_merchant`'s FOUR.** No `GoogleAdsLink`: the link comes
from a consent the merchant completes, and a row asserting a link nobody
authorised is precisely what `create_merchant`'s docstring refuses. No
`BusinessProfile` either - onboarding writes that from the crawl it does
itself. The `GuardrailConfig` IS written, from limits the merchant agreed
to on the way in.

**A LINKLESS MERCHANT CANNOT SPEND, AND NOT BECAUSE OF ANYTHING HERE.**
`guardrails.check_link_valid` calls `_require(c.link_status, ...)`, which
raises `_Unevaluable` on `None`, so check 1 fail-closes before anything
reaches Google. The safety property was enforced before this endpoint
existed; this docstring records where it comes from so nobody re-implements
it as a status column.

The console sends the merchant to `/start?merchant_id=...` next, which is
unchanged - there is no new contract with the OAuth half.

schema.title: Response Sign Up Api Signups Post

post.description:
Run the simulated world forward, then let the optimization loop see it.

**ADVANCING THE CALENDAR WITHOUT RUNNING THE LOOP WOULD SHOW A CLIENT
NOTHING.** The rules read the store, the store is filled by ingestion, and
ingestion reads the days the auction has generated - so the three are one
act from a demo's point of view, and splitting them into three endpoints
would make "advance 30 days" appear to do nothing at all.

Every merchant with a linked account and a campaign we know about is swept.
One merchant's failure is reported and does not stop the others - see
`ppcway.api.optimizing`.

schema.title: Response Sim Advance Api Sim Advance Post

post.description:
Approve (or un-approve) billing at Google, and mirror it onto the link.

**BOTH HALVES, AND THE SECOND IS NOT BOOKKEEPING.** `check_billing_ready`
reads `GoogleAdsLink.billing_status`, which is PPCWay's MIRROR of a fact
Google owns - and nothing in `src/` syncs it (the account-health poll reads
it rather than writing it). So the mirror is written at the moment Google's
original is changed, exactly as `ppcway.acceptance.story._billing` does it,
and `docs/ACCEPTANCE.md` names that as a limitation rather than letting it
look like a sync.

schema.title: Response Sim Billing Api Sim Billing Post

post.description:
Record that a conversion has been seen end to end. Story step 6.

A PPCWay row rather than a simulator one, because what it records is that WE
saw the conversion arrive: Google's own conversion action is a different
fact, and conflating them is how a platform tells a merchant their tracking
works when it has never seen a lead. `decide_bidding` refuses a launch
without one (§13.5's gate, which does not bend for volume), so this is what
turns that refusal into a launch.
